sections.overview: Native across much of Europe and western Eurasia, the European pine marten varies greatly in abundance and local range. It climbs and forages extensively on the forest floor.
sections.identification: Adults have rich brown fur, a yellow to orange bib on the throat and chest, pale-edged ears and a long, bushy tail. The bib’s colour and outline vary among populations and individuals. Males average larger than females; European samples report adult masses of about 0.8–2.4 kilograms for males and 0.6–1.5 kilograms for females, with ranges varying among studies. The beech marten usually has a white bib that forks toward the forelegs and a pale nose; the pine marten usually has a yellowish bib and dark nose.
sections.habitat: The species uses coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests; mature stands are valuable where they provide canopy cover and cavities in old trees or standing deadwood. These structures offer cover and secure resting or breeding sites. In an Irish landscape with few tree cavities, monitored martens also denned in caves, rock crevices, stone walls and wood debris, while avoiding most immature plantations.
sections.diet: The pine marten is an opportunistic omnivore: small mammals, birds and eggs, carrion, invertebrates and fruit all feature in its diet. In Northern Ireland, scat analyses found animal foods prominent in spring and summer and berries important in autumn; birds and small mammals became more important when fruit was scarce. In Galloway, no carrion was detected in denning females’ scats; birds, small mammals and anurans were important, unlike some carrion-containing mixed-sex spring diets reported elsewhere in Scotland.
sections.behavior: Pine martens are usually solitary outside mating and mostly nocturnal, though activity varies with season. Scent marks, including conspicuously placed scats, signal occupancy along routes; Spanish observations found marking concentrated at exposed sites and crossroads, especially in May and July. British studies found larger home ranges in males than females, with estimates varying among habitats and food conditions.
sections.reproduction: Mating in July–August is followed by about seven months of delayed implantation. Implantation in late winter is followed by 30–35 days of development; births occur in late March or April. Females usually have one litter of one to five kits each year. Born blind, deaf and toothless, kits open their eyes at 34–38 days, eat solids from 36–45 days and are weaned at about six weeks. Young emerge at 7–8 weeks; dispersal may start at 12–16 weeks, though some overwinter in their natal territory and leave the following spring. Females use protected dens during the early weeks.
sections.ecology: After eating fleshy fruits, pine martens can carry seeds away from parent shrubs in their scats. In a temperate-forest experiment, marked seed mimics embedded in fruit were recovered up to 1,233 metres from feeding stations, a study maximum rather than a typical distance. In the Irish midlands, surveys recorded grey-squirrel decline alongside red-squirrel return where martens recovered. Later analyses across Britain and Ireland found regional associations between marten exposure, lower grey-squirrel occupancy and higher red-squirrel occupancy. In an Irish feeder-camera study, red squirrels became more vigilant and fed less after a marten visit; this short-lived response is a possible mechanism, not proof of the population pattern. These patterns do not show that martens eliminate grey squirrels everywhere or always benefit red squirrels.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classified the species as Least Concern globally in an assessment dated 3 March 2015 and published in 2016, citing its wide range and large population despite past declines. This global category does not describe every national population: the Mammal Society lists Great Britain as Least Concern, while martens remain scarce in parts of England and Wales amid habitat fragmentation and persecution. Across Great Britain, the amended Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 protects the species, with schedule coverage varying by jurisdiction. Ireland separately lists the pine marten under its Wildlife Act 1976.
